summary.text: In Japanese, 日 writes the sun, daylight, and a day; its ancient graph is a picture of the sun. Japanese readings include ひ and the borrowed on-readings ニチ and ジツ.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts the sun. Paleographic interpretation describes early rounded forms, sometimes squared in carving, with a central mark distinguishing 日 from 囗. The later Shuowen analysis divides it into 囗 and 一, but earlier evidence does not establish these as original components.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze examples attest the graph in early inscriptional traditions. The documented script categories also include Chu manuscript and seal forms, but the available evidence does not date every form or establish a detailed graphic sequence.
The received Han-era Shuowen account analyzes 日 as 从囗一: an outline and an inner stroke. This records a later interpretation of the graph, not proof that those were its original components.
The Japanese graph is written 日; the supplied evidence does not identify a separate kyūjitai counterpart or a 日-specific shinjitai change.

uncertainties.text: The cited Shang-period inscriptions attest uses for the sun, daylight, a five-day period, and a sacrificial name, but do not establish their relative order or all semantic links. Exact dates for individual inscriptions were not independently verified.
The evidence does not date the emergence of the rounded and squared forms or the central mark, nor give a detailed sequence of graphic changes.

The Japanese historical dictionary records Japanese uses and dated examples, but these do not establish a continuous semantic path from the early Chinese inscriptions. The first use of isolated 日 as an abbreviation for 日本 is also unresolved in the supplied research.

senses.text: Oracle-bone examples attest 日 for the sun. This is a use in the earliest documented corpus cited here, not proof of the graph's first-ever use.
Oracle-bone examples use 日 for daylight, including in contrast with evening. Whether this use developed from the sun sense is not established.
An oracle-bone example attests 日 for a five-day period. The evidence does not establish when or how this use relates to the sun and daylight uses.
The cited corpus includes 日 as a sacrificial name. Its relation, if any, to the sun, daylight, or day-unit uses is not established.

senses.period: Japanese word ひ; earliest cited example in 古事記 (712)
senses.text: The Japanese historical dictionary cites ひ（日） for the sun in 古事記 (712). This is an attestation of the Japanese word, not a date for the ancient Chinese graph.

senses.period: Japanese word ひ; earliest cited example in 万葉集 (late 8th century)
senses.text: The Japanese historical dictionary cites ひ（日） for sunlight in the 万葉集, from the late eighth century.

senses.period: Japanese word ひ; cited example in 古事記 (712)
senses.text: The Japanese historical dictionary cites ひ（日） for daytime in 古事記 (712). Its evidence does not connect this Japanese use chronologically to the Shang inscriptional senses.

senses.gloss: day as a unit of time
senses.period: Japanese word ひ; cited example in 三教指帰 (c. 797)
senses.text: A Japanese historical dictionary cites 一日 in 三教指帰 (c. 797) for a day as a time unit.

senses.period: Japanese word ひ; cited example in 竹取物語 (late 9th to early 10th century)
senses.text: A Japanese historical dictionary cites a specified-date use in 竹取物語, dated to the late ninth or early tenth century.
Japanese character-dictionary data lists Japan among the meanings associated with 日, but the supplied evidence does not establish the history or first date of this single-character use.

senses.gloss: counter for calendar dates or elapsed days
senses.text: Japanese reference data records 日 as a counter for dates and elapsed days; the cited materials do not establish its development from the ancient Chinese uses.

limitations.text: The early inscriptions document several uses but do not establish their relative chronology or transitions. Shared early attestation does not show that one sense developed from another.
The Japanese historical dictionary provides dated examples for Japanese words and uses, but they do not establish a continuous semantic path from the early Chinese graph.
The supplied research does not establish when 日 alone began to abbreviate 日本; the attested history of 日本 is not by itself evidence for that abbreviation's first date.

overview.text: 日 is a picture of the sun. Japanese uses it for the sun and a day, with readings such as ひ and ニチ; early inscriptions also attest daylight and a five-day unit.

summary.text: Japanese 日 has native kun readings such as ひ and borrowed on-readings ニチ and ジツ. The official reading table also lists か; word-level readings such as きょう in 今日 belong to whole words.

readings.text: The kun reading associates the character with the Japanese word for sun; here it appears in 日光.
A common on-reading in compounds; listed in the official Japanese reading table and used in 毎日.
Another on-reading, listed in the official Japanese reading table and used in 日曜日.
